items.title: Base-ten place values
items.content: From right to left: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, and so on. Each place is ten times the place to its right. A digit’s value is digit × place value.

items.title: Reading, rounding and notation
items.content: Face value is the digit itself; place value depends on position. Indian grouping uses lakh/crore; international grouping uses million/billion. Round by checking the digit immediately to the right of the target place.

items.title: Exam checks
items.content:
Read the whole number aloud to check its grouping.
Use expanded form when a digit’s value is unclear.

items.title: Face value and place value
items.content: Worked example: in 5,47,326, the face value of 7 is 7; its place value is 7,000 because it is in the thousands place.

items.title: Expanded form
items.content: Worked example: 8,03,052 = \(8\times100000+3\times1000+5\times10+2\). Zero placeholders mark empty places.

items.title: Compare and order numbers
items.content: Compare the number of digits first, then the leftmost unequal digit. Worked example: 5,08,900 > 4,99,999 because the lakh digit is larger.

items.title: Regrouping and carrying
items.content: Ten units of a place make one unit of the next. Worked example: 2,758 + 1,486 = 4,244 after regrouping ones, tens and hundreds.

items.title: Rounding numbers
items.content: Worked example: round 7,46,582 to nearest thousand. Hundreds digit is 5, so round up to 7,47,000.

items.title: Indian and international grouping
items.content: The same number may be written 12,34,567 (Indian) or 1,234,567 (international); value does not change. Read the named grouping carefully. Worked example: 12,34,567 and 1,234,567 denote the same value: one million two hundred thirty-four thousand five hundred sixty-seven.

items.title: Find the value of a digit
items.content: Worked example: in 63,418, the 3 has value 3,000 and face value 3.

items.title: Compare or arrange numbers
items.content: Compare from the highest place; zeros are meaningful placeholders. Worked example: 6,020 > 5,999 because 6 thousands exceed 5 thousands.

items.title: Round to a stated place
items.content: Mark the target digit, inspect the next digit, then replace all lower places by zeros. Worked example: 4,786 rounded to the nearest hundred is 4,800.

items.title: Use place value in calculations
items.content: Check each regrouped unit remains equivalent: 10 tens become 1 hundred. Worked example: 368 + 257 = 625; regroup 15 ones as 1 ten and 5 ones.

items.title: Why each place is ten times the next
items.content: In base ten, a digit’s value is multiplied by \(10^k\) at position \(k\). Moving one place left multiplies its value by 10.

items.title: Why a zero placeholder matters
items.content: Zero contributes no quantity in its own place but keeps digits in their correct positions; removing it may change the number by a factor of ten or more.

items.title: Why rounding uses the next digit
items.content: The next digit determines whether the value is closer to the target multiple or the next one; digits farther right do not change that nearest-place decision.

sections.title: Common errors and how to avoid them

items.title: Confusing face and place value
items.content: Face value is the digit; place value includes its position.

items.title: Dropping placeholder zeros
items.content: Keep zeros needed to preserve positions in standard form.

items.title: Rounding the wrong digit
items.content: Look one place to the right of the rounding place.

items.title: Mixing number grouping systems
items.content: Use separators and names consistently; commas do not change numerical value.

keyTakeaways: Place value is positional and base ten.
Zero can be a placeholder without contributing a quantity.
Rounding depends on the digit immediately after the target place.
Indian and international commas group the same value differently.
